newsitem.title: USA: New guide untangles mysteries of baby products.
newsitem.headline: New guide untangles mysteries of baby products.

text.p: Babies, wonderful as they may be, have an innate ability to discover the potential for danger in any object.
Across the country, parents and other relatives spend more than $10 billion a year on baby products, including more than $638 million on toys.
But just because a product is designed for a baby is no guarantee that the product will be appropriate or safe -- or that the parent will use it properly.

"Thousands of babies are injured each year in accidents related to baby products because parents overestimate the protective qualities imparted by manufacturers to their products," writes "Guide to Baby Products," from Consumer Reports Books ($14.95, $21 Canadian).

In this new, comprehensive guide to baby products, Consumer Reports looks at products from backpacks to gates, high chairs to toilet learning aids and rates them according to safety, ease of use and price.
The book is designed to help adults see through advertising hype or peer pressure and select baby products that meet safety, convenience and price criteria.
"Safety is the No. 1 issue when selecting baby products," said Sandy Jones, the book's co-author with Werner Freitag and the editors of Consumer Reports books.

"Over 100,000 babies a year are sent to emergency rooms in product-related accidents," she said from her home in Brevard, N.C. The potential for danger is often not evident until accidents occur -- a perfectly safe-looking toy box can have a cover that snaps shut or a high-chair can have sharp edges.
Jones said parents must select products that serve their intended purposes, not cause more problems than they solve.

Purchasers of a wide variety of baby products can look for Juvenile Products Manufacturers Association (JPMA) or American Society for Testing Materials certification stickers on an item as one test for quality, but "standards are different for different products."
The baby products business "is a very complex business," she said. "There are no clear standards. Federal regulations are voluntary for many of the products."

When looking at strollers, for example, Jones said one stroller might have a certification sticker and a similar one may not. A parent then has to become an investigator, checking out the stroller's safety features as well as checking with various organisations to research whether there have been any product recalls.
Jones, who has studied hundreds of infant accidents, said "baby product manufacturers in the past have made too large an issue of the fact that parents don't use products correctly."
Indeed parents need "a clear dose of reality so as not to rely on products to be babysitters... No product is fail-safe," she said.
But when you see the same accident occuring time and time again with the same product, "you see that the design of the product is wrong."

Some specific products should always be viewed with caution, such as walkers, safety gates and hook-on high chairs. Walkers, or wheeled baby seats, have been clocked up at speeds of up to 35 miles per hour; some safety gates can be easily dislodged from door jams and hook-on high chairs can fall off.
In addition, between 40 percent and 90 percent of parents fail to install child car seats properly.
Is it a problem with the parent, or is it also a problem with the product's design?
While the courts decide the answers, Jones advises parents to take an active role in assuring that the products they purchase for their children will be the safest available.

When shopping for baby products, Jones advises parents "take the product off the self, remove it from the box, touch it and feel it. Look for sharp edges, dangerous hinges, latches on safety belts" and keep in mind any potential for choking, strangulation, suffocation, finger entrapment or burns.
Also carefully read the warning literature inside the box.
Jones said that a baby toy with a battery might seem totally innocuous, but after reading the warning on the battery parents might change their minds.

"Also, follow the specific age guidelines" on a toy, game or product, no matter how intellectually advanced a child might be. The guidelines are designed to help keep toys with small parts away from toddlers.
To order "Guide to Baby Products" by Consumer Reports Books, call 1-800-500-9760.

For current recalls of child safety seats call the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) at 1-800-424-9393; for recalls on other baby products call the Consumer Product Safety Commission's Product Safety Hotline at 1-800-638-2772. For information on baby formula, baby food and skin-care product recalls, call the Consumer Inquiries Hotline of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration at 1-800-332-4010.
